title: Rural life: I am eternally grateful to my alcoholic father
gist: In a personal essay, Kiran Sidhu argues her alcoholic father was nonetheless a good parent because his visible, human failures taught her early that adults are fallible and that authenticity in a flawed parent can be more developmentally valuable than curated inauthenticity.

insights.claim: The author frames addiction as never contained to the individual sufferer — it spreads outward to affect the whole family, which is why her father's alcoholism was 'our family's problem' rather than just his own.
insights.speaker: Kiran Sidhu
insights.so_what: A general framework for assessing addiction's impact: treat it as a household-level condition rather than an individual one when evaluating family or social outcomes.
insights.quote: This is always the case with addiction; the problem is never contained to the one person suffering with the disease, but instead seeps outwards, affecting everyone around the person.
insights.locator: Throughout my life, my father battled with alcoholism

insights.claim: Growing up with a visibly flawed, 'Jekyll and Hyde' parent taught the author early that adults are not infallible and that the world is not black and white, which she credits with reinforcing her own strength of character rather than damaging her.
insights.speaker: Kiran Sidhu
insights.so_what: Pushes back against the default assumption that visible parental dysfunction is purely harmful, suggesting early exposure to adult fallibility can build resilience.
insights.quote: I understood from a very young age that adults weren't infallible. This reinforced my own strength of character.
insights.locator: You might expect the child of a parent with a 'Jekyll and Hyde' personality

insights.claim: The author's father deliberately chose to take her to see 'Gandhi' instead of 'ET' at age nine specifically to teach her about political revolutions, and she credits this single choice as the origin of her lifelong interest in politics.
insights.speaker: Kiran Sidhu
insights.so_what: An example of how a single deliberate parental media choice can causally shape a lifelong intellectual interest, illustrating outsized long-run effects from small, specific parenting decisions.
insights.quote: my father thought it was more important that I understood how political revolutions happened
insights.locator: The first film my father took his kids to watch in the cinema was Gandhi

insights.claim: The author's broader claim is that a parent's visible authenticity, including visible failures, can be more valuable to a child's development than a parent's curated inauthenticity.
insights.speaker: Kiran Sidhu
insights.so_what: A general framework applicable beyond parenting: transparency about flaws may build more durable trust/understanding than a polished but inauthentic presentation.
insights.quote: I would rather live life truthfully in all its messiness than approach it wearing rubber gloves.
insights.locator: I reflect on how extraordinarily real his failures made him
